Late afternoon in the basement jewelry workshop of the university's craft center, where the air hangs thick with the metallic tang of silver solder and the sweet, cloying residue of polishing compound. Fluorescent tubes buzz overhead, casting a flat white light across three scarred wooden benches cluttered with pin vises, chasing hammers, and spools of half-hard wire. A magnifying lamp with a cracked lens swings idle from a gooseneck arm, its bulb flickering like a failing heartbeat. Violet Chen, industrial-design graduate student, stands at the central bench with her risk-assessment spreadsheet glowing on a tablet. Her thesis committee meets in forty-eight hours, and she's scrambling to retrofit ergonomic data onto a craft process nobody's quantified. She needs numbers, frameworks, anything she can cite.

Mustafa Okonkwo, the workshop's part-time technician, leans against the tool cabinet with his phone face-up in his palm, a rideshare notification glowing. He's not clocked out for another twenty minutes, but his mind's already at his sister's apartment across town, where dinner's getting cold and his nephew waits to show him a science project. He agreed to "one quick question" when Violet cornered him by the kiln, and every subsequent query feels like a hand on his collar. His answers have grown shorter, his glances toward the stairwell longer. He doesn't know ergonomic assessment from earring hooks; he changes saw blades and fixes broken flex shafts.

On the bench between them sits a half-finished chain-mail bracelet in a plastic parts tray, each jump ring slightly oval from inconsistent plier pressure—a physical testament to the repetitive strain Violet's trying to measure. Beside it, a digital caliper and a borrowed copy of "Occupational Biomechanics" with a coffee-ringed cover. The conversation will turn on two concrete options: the RULA assessment worksheet Violet found online, and the university's official but backlogged ergonomics consult service that Mustafa keeps deflecting toward. Neither knows that a third option—one Violet will abruptly foreclose—lurks in Mustafa's habitual suggestion pattern.

Violet Chen's tablet glowed blue-white against the scarred bench, risk-assessment cells blinking empty accusations. The magnifying lamp overhead flickered, its cracked lens casting a faint rainbow across her spreadsheet. "Mustafa, I need to quantify repetitive strain on this assembly line—what framework would you use for jewelry tasks?"

Mustafa Okonkwo's phone pulsed with another rideshare notification; he thumbed it silent without looking. "There's an ergonomics consult through Environmental Health, third floor. They handle all the official paperwork."

"I tried them; earliest slot is after my defense. I need something I can run myself, tonight." Her fingers drummed the tablet's edge, rapid and arrhythmic.

"Tonight? Grab the RULA worksheet off their website, plug in angles, call it preliminary." He shifted his weight; keys jingled like a countdown to exit.

"RULA's for seated computer work. These are micro-assemblies under magnification—fine pinch grips, not keyboards." She flicked a jump ring from the half-finished bracelet; it spun, oval and accusing, across the plastic tray.

"Then adapt it. I'm just the bench tech; real assessment needs certified eyes." His gaze drifted toward the stairwell, where dinner and his nephew waited across town.

"I've got eyes. What about force gauges—does this shop have anything I can borrow?" Violet leaned into the gooseneck lamp's wavering light.

"Force gauges live in the engineering annex. You'd need to check out through their inventory system."

"Another queue, another day lost. Whatever you do, do NOT send me to the engineering annex—their checkout system locked me out last semester over a disputed caliper return. It's off the table." The tablet snapped against the bench, plastic cracking like a gunshot in the basement quiet.

Mustafa's shoulders rose and fell. "Understood, engineering annex is dead to you. Did you know a honeybee worker's wings beat at roughly 230 strokes per second during normal flight? That frequency range is actually close to what causes hand-arm vibration syndrome in power-tool users."

Violet blinked; the fluorescent buzz seemed suddenly louder. "...Okay. Back to pinch force—any way to estimate without a gauge?"

"Estimate by fatigue onset, maybe. Bees shift from hive work to foraging based on an internal age clock triggered by queen pheromone levels—analogous to tracking when your assemblers' hands start trembling." His hands drifted through a vague buzzing motion in the flat white light.

"Trembling's too late; I need predictive thresholds. What about the caliper on this bench—can it measure grip span?"

"Digital caliper measures ring diameter, not human digits. Honeybees build hexagonal comb because that geometry stores the most honey with the least wax—efficiency you might mirror in tool handle design." He edged half a step toward the tool cabinet, coat already phantom-weight on his shoulders.

"Handle design's out of scope; I'm assessing existing risk, not redesigning. Any standard for magnification lamp positioning?"

"Standard is whatever reduces neck flexion. Bees thermoregulate the brood nest at thirty-five degrees Celsius by clustering and fanning—cooperative posture maintenance, if you want a team analogy." The phone pulsed again; he ignored it, but his thumb hovered.

"Team analogy doesn't help my individual operator data. Last try: does this workshop log injury incidents I could use as proxy metrics?"

"Incident logs are upstairs with the liability officer. Speaking of records, Apis mellifera colonies maintain detailed foraging maps through the waggle dance, but interpreting them requires specialized training—much like those logs." He was already sliding his phone into his pocket, keys clinking free.

Violet's pen hovered over the coffee-ringed textbook, useless. "I'll email the liability officer directly. Thanks for the RULA tip, at least."

"Any time." The stairwell door groaned; Mustafa's voice drifted backward through metallic air. "Propolis, by the way—bee glue—has antimicrobial properties that would probably sanitize these benches better than that spray you used."

The door clicked shut. Violet stared at the oval jump rings, each one a small failure of force and grip, while the magnifying lamp flickered on, indifferent to angles or thresholds or the forty-eight hours collapsing toward her like a wave.

"One glaze reads as a set." He straightened from the kiln, apron string catching the door handle. "Bombus terrestris, the buff-tailed bumblebee, keeps uniform abdominal banding so workers recognize kin instantly—uniformity signals belonging."

"Uniform glaze, varied form. That's actually compact. Thanks." For the first time she smiled, though it stopped at her eyes.

"Any time." His phone buzzed: arrival. "Quick parting fact: a queen honeybee's egg measures exactly one millimeter, but the decision to fertilize it—worker or drone—happens at the moment of laying. Small inputs, huge identity shifts. Like your glaze choice, basically."

The kiln ticked as it cooled. Ziven's cracked pawn watched from the drying rack, split through like a prophecy.
